title: VonNeumann
body:
The **stored-program** architecture: instructions and data live in the same
[[Main memory]], reachable over the same [[Bus]]. The [[Motorola 68000]] is one, and so is
essentially every machine you will use.

The parts, as the model states them:

- a [[CPU]] holding a control unit and an [[ALU]]
- one memory holding both the program and its data
- [[I-O]] to reach the outside world
- a [[Bus]] connecting them

## Why it matters that code is data

Because the machine cannot tell them apart, only the program counter's history decides which
bits get executed. That single fact explains:

- **Compilers, assemblers, and loaders** can exist at all. A program that writes another
  program is just a program writing bytes. See [[Assembly]].
- **Illegal instruction** faults. Jump somewhere wrong and the 68000 will happily try to
  execute your string constant, four bombs later. See [[Assembly Errors]].
- **Buffer overflow attacks**, the same trick done on purpose.

## The Von Neumann bottleneck

One bus, shared. The [[CPU]] can fetch an instruction or fetch data, not both at once, so
memory bandwidth caps the machine no matter how fast the processor gets. Since
[[Main memory]] is already slower than the CPU, this is the gap that [[Cache]] exists to
paper over, and the reason processor speed alone stopped being the interesting number.

The alternative is **Harvard architecture**: separate instruction and data memories with
separate buses, so a fetch and a load happen in parallel. Microcontrollers and DSPs use it,
and modern CPUs are Von Neumann in the large but split their L1 [[Cache]] into instruction
and data halves, which is Harvard where it counts.
